verdict.rationale: Two text-grounded lexical patterns coexist and the vocabulary does not rank them. Pattern A, ongoing conscious punishment: 'they will be tormented' (basanisthesontai) 'unto the ages of the ages' (eis tous aionas ton aionon) in Revelation 20:10, paired with 'they have no rest day and night' (ouk echousin anapausin hemeras kai nyktos) in Revelation 14:11, the durative (ongoing) double negation 'does not die' (ou teleuta) and 'is not quenched' (ou sbennytai) in Mark 9:48, and the strict grammatical parallel of 'eternal punishment' (kolasin aionion) with 'eternal life' (zoen aionion) in Matthew 25:46 where one adjective 'eternal' (aionios) governs both nouns. Pattern B, terminal destruction or cessation: the active 'to destroy' (apolesai) of both 'soul' (psyche) and 'body' (soma) in 'hell' (gehenna) in Matthew 10:28, with 'destroy' (apollymi) attested 93 times across the New Testament and ordinarily denoting ruin or loss, 'eternal destruction' (olethron aionion) in 2 Thessalonians 1:9, the 'destruction' (apoleia) word-group (19 New Testament occurrences, Philippians 3:19, 2 Peter 3:7), the explicit gloss (plain-English explanation) of the lake of fire as 'the second death' (ho thanatos ho deuteros) in Revelation 20:14, and the canon's reservation of 'immortality' (athanasia, Strong's G0110, 3 occurrences) and 'incorruption' (aphtharsia) for the redeemed alone, with Daniel 12:2 carrying 'abhorrence' (deraon), a hapax-class noun (a word that occurs essentially only once in the Bible) shared only with Isaiah 66:24 whose imagery acts on 'corpses' (pegarim). The pivotal adjective 'eternal' (aionios, 69 New Testament occurrences, 71 with anchor count) is genuinely two-valued, lexically durative (ongoing in time) in some contexts and qualitative of the coming age in others. Both patterns are defensible from the words on the page, so the lexical evidence supports the stem on its strongest texts but is materially contested by the destruction vocabulary.

scripture.force: The verb 'they will be tormented' (basanisthesontai) is future passive of 'to torment' (basanizo), and is governed by the unbounded temporal phrase 'unto the ages of the ages' (eis tous aionas ton aionon), the strongest duration formula the canon possesses. The grammatical subject is a personal triad: 'the devil' (ho diabolos), 'the beast' (to therion), 'the false prophet' (ho pseudoprophetes), already cast 'into the lake of fire' (eis ten limnen tou pyros). A future passive verb of torment with an open-ended ages-of-ages phrase reads most naturally as durative (ongoing) experience, not instantaneous extinction. This is the strongest single text for the stem.

'The smoke of their torment goes up unto ages of ages' (ho kapnos tou basanismou auton eis aionas aionon anabainei), coupled with 'they have no rest day and night' (ouk echousin anapausin hemeras kai nyktos). The negated 'rest' (anapausis) with the merism (a two-part figure naming the extremes to mean the whole) 'day and night' (hemeras kai nyktos) predicates an unceasing experiential state of the worshippers. This favors the stem. The rising-smoke image also draws on Isaiah 34:10 (Edom) and Genesis 19:28 (Sodom), where the smoke marks a completed destruction whose memorial endures, which is why the verse is also pressed by the destruction reading.

'Eternal punishment' (kolasin aionion) stands in strict syntactic parallel with 'eternal life' (zoen aionion) within a single antithetic (contrasting) clause, the lone adjective 'eternal' (aionios) governing both nouns. The construction means whatever duration is predicated of the life is predicated of the punishment. The complication is lexical, not syntactic: whether 'punishment' (kolasis, only 2 New Testament occurrences, here and 1 John 4:18) denotes the ongoing act of punishing or the resultant state of having been punished, and whether 'eternal' (aionios) is durative (lasting forever) or qualitative (belonging to the coming age).

Two coordinated negated present-tense verbs (ongoing simple statements of fact), 'their worm does not die and the fire is not quenched' (ho skolex auton ou teleuta kai to pyr ou sbennytai), assert perpetuity of the agents of judgment. The clause is a direct citation of Isaiah 66:24 in the Greek Old Testament (the Septuagint, LXX). Whether the perpetuity attaches to a conscious sufferer or only to the unquenchable means of destruction is exactly the disputed point, because the source text describes the agents working on dead bodies. The text fixes the agents as undying and unquenched but does not by itself fix the object's mode of presence.

The resurrection of 'the many' (rabbim) divides into 'to everlasting life' (lechayye olam) and 'to reproach and everlasting abhorrence' (lecherpot ledeeraon olam). The single qualifier 'everlasting' (olam) stands over both destinies in poetic parallel, so the duration assigned to the 'life' (chayyim) of the righteous is the duration assigned to the 'reproach' (cherpah) and 'abhorrence' (deraon) of the wicked. The noun 'abhorrence' (deraon) is a hapax-class lexeme (a word occurring essentially only once in the Bible), occurring only here and in Isaiah 66:24, binding the Daniel resurrection oracle directly to the worm-and-fire imagery. The post-resurrection setting argues against simple cessation, but 'abhorrence' (deraon) denotes abhorrence or aversion (something looked upon) rather than torment, so the term does not by itself specify ongoing consciousness of the abhorred.

The source-image quoted by Mark 9:48. The onlookers gaze on the 'corpses' (pegarim) of the rebels, whose worm does not die and whose fire is not quenched. The objects of the undying worm and unquenched fire are explicitly dead bodies ('corpses', pegarim, root 'pgr', a strong concrete noun for slain corpses), not living conscious persons. This is the principal lexical anchor for the destruction reading, because the deathless worm consumes the slain rather than tormenting the awake. A durative (ongoing) reading must argue that the New Testament transposes the imagery from completed slaughter to a conscious post-resurrection state.

'To destroy' (apolesai) active aorist infinitive (a completed-action infinitive) with God as agent and both 'soul' (psyche) and 'body' (soma) as direct objects in 'hell' (gehenna). The verb 'destroy' (apollymi) occurs 93 times across the New Testament and carries a sense-range from render-lost or ruin (John 6:12 of fragments, John 17:12 'the son of destruction' (ho huios tes apoleias)) to destroy or put to death (Matthew 2:13 Herod seeks the child 'to destroy' (apolesai), Matthew 27:20). The collocation here, 'to destroy' (apolesai) both soul and body in 'hell' (gehenna) with God as agent, sits at the destruction end of the range. The eternal-torment reading takes 'destroy' (apollymi) here in the metaphorical sense of ruining a person's flourishing without extinguishing existence; the destruction reading takes it at the strong sense of putting out of existence. The lexeme allows both, with the 'hell' (gehenna) context pressing toward the strong sense without forcing it.

'Eternal destruction away from the face of the Lord' (olethron aionion apo prosopou tou kyriou). The head noun is 'destruction' (olethros, 4 New Testament occurrences: here, 1 Corinthians 5:5, 1 Thessalonians 5:3, 1 Timothy 6:9), a destruction or ruin word, not a torment word. A destruction reading takes 'eternal' (aionios) as qualifying an irreversible outcome, eternal in result. A durative (ongoing) reading answers that 'eternal' (aionios) in 2 Thessalonians 1:9 functions adjectivally as in Matthew 25:46 and need not collapse into cessation; 'destruction' (olethros) can denote ruinous separation from the Lord's presence (the prepositional phrase 'away from the face' (apo prosopou)) rather than extinction. The lexeme alone does not decide.

'Death and Hades were cast into the lake of fire. This is the second death, the lake of fire' (ho thanatos kai ho hades eblethesan eis ten limnen tou pyros. houtos ho thanatos ho deuteros estin, he limne tou pyros). The text supplies an explicit lexical gloss (plain-English equation): the lake of fire IS 'the second death' (thanatos). 'Death' (thanatos) is the canon's primary death word (120 New Testament occurrences) and ordinarily denotes the cessation of biological life. The destruction reading presses this as a decisive identification: whatever the lake of fire is, the apostle defines it as a death, not as an unending vital state. The eternal-torment reading answers that Revelation 20:10 has just predicated unending torment of the personal triad cast into the same lake, so 'second death' (deuteros thanatos) must be a metaphorical death-state of ongoing alienation rather than literal cessation. The gloss is real and the reconciliation must be argued.

'For this corruptible must put on incorruption, and this mortal must put on immortality' (dei gar to phtharton touto endusasthai aphtharsian kai to thneton touto endusasthai athanasian). The terms 'immortality' (athanasia, 3 New Testament occurrences: here, 1 Corinthians 15:54, 1 Timothy 6:16 of God alone) and 'incorruption' (aphtharsia) are predicated of the redeemed at the resurrection. The destruction reading takes the canon's restriction of 'immortality' (athanasia) to God and to the redeemed (conditional immortality, the view that unending life is given only to believers) as a structural argument that the unredeemed do not naturally possess unending existence. The eternal-torment reading answers that 'immortality' (athanasia) is here a positive-quality term for the glorified body, not a metaphysical claim that the lost cease to exist. The text supports conditional immortality lexically without contradicting either eschatology (end-times view).

'For the wages of sin is death, but the gift of God is eternal life' (ta gar opsonia tes hamartias thanatos, to de charisma tou theou zoe aionios). The Pauline antithesis (Paul's contrast) sets 'death' (thanatos) against 'eternal life' (zoe aionios), not against 'eternal life of torment' (zoe basanismou aioniou). The contrast term for unending life is death itself. The destruction reading takes this as the canon's own lexical opposition. The eternal-torment reading takes 'death' (thanatos) here as the present consequence of sin (compare Romans 5:12) leaving the mode of the final state to be specified by other texts. The asymmetry is real: the wage of sin is not named as eternal punishment but as death.

complicating_texts.resolution: The undying worm and unquenched fire in the Markan source act on 'corpses' (pegarim). A durative (ongoing) reading must argue that Mark transposes the imagery from completed slaughter onto the conscious post-resurrection state, since Daniel 12:2, which shares the rare noun 'abhorrence' (deraon) with Isaiah 66:24, locates the abhorrence after resurrection. The transfer is plausible but not lexically forced, which is part of why the verdict is disputed.

'Eternal destruction' (olethron aionion). 'Destruction' (olethros, 4 New Testament occurrences) denotes ruin or destruction, not torment. A destruction reading takes 'eternal' (aionios) here as qualifying an irreversible outcome, eternal in result. A durative (ongoing) reading takes 'destruction' (olethros) as ruinous separation from the Lord's presence ('away from the face', apo prosopou) rather than extinction, with 'eternal' (aionios) functioning adverbially as in Matthew 25:46. Neither reading is lexically excluded.

'To destroy' (apolesai) active aorist (completed-action) form of 'destroy' (apollymi) with God as agent and both 'soul' (psyche) and 'body' (soma) as objects in 'hell' (gehenna). The verb's 93-occurrence New Testament range spans render-lost (John 6:12 of fragments) and put-to-death (Matthew 2:13 of Herod's intent toward the child), so the verbal sense in Matthew 10:28 is genuinely two-valued. The 'hell' (gehenna) setting and the collocation of soul-and-body presses toward the strong sense (extinction of the whole person) without lexically forcing it, since 'destroy' (apollymi) is also used metaphorically of ruined flourishing in the Johannine 'lose oneself' idiom. This is the strongest single destruction-language datum against the stem.

'This is the second death, the lake of fire' (houtos ho thanatos ho deuteros estin, he limne tou pyros). The clause identifies the lake of fire as the second death ('death', thanatos, the canon's primary cessation-of-life word). A destruction reading takes the apostle's own gloss as decisive: the final state IS a death. A durative (ongoing) reading must argue that Revelation 20:10, which predicates 'they will be tormented unto the ages of the ages' (basanisthesontai eis tous aionas ton aionon) of the personal triad in the same lake, forces a metaphorical sense of 'death' (thanatos) here (separation, alienation from the source of life) rather than cessation. The text supplies the gloss and supplies the tension simultaneously.

The canon attests 'immortality' (athanasia, Strong's G0110, 3 occurrences) only of God (1 Timothy 6:16) and of the redeemed at resurrection (1 Corinthians 15:53 to 54). A conditional-immortality (immortality-as-gift) reading takes this restriction as structural: the unredeemed do not naturally possess unending existence, so destruction of the lost is the default lexical expectation. A durative (ongoing) reading takes 'immortality' (athanasia) as a positive-quality term for glorified bodily life, not a metaphysical claim about who exists. Both can be sustained; the texts say what they say about the redeemed and leave the negative case to inference.

'Death' (thanatos) against 'eternal life' (zoe aionios). The Pauline antithesis (Paul's contrast) names the wage of sin as 'death' (thanatos), not as 'eternal punishment' (kolasis aionios) or 'torment' (basanismos). A destruction reading takes the contrast term as the canon's own naming of the negative outcome: death, not unending pain. A durative (ongoing) reading reads 'death' (thanatos) here as the present penalty of sin (Romans 5:12) whose final mode is specified by other texts (Revelation 14:11, 20:10). The lexical asymmetry is real and is recorded honestly.

variant_units_examined.note: Verses 44 and 46, which repeat the worm-and-fire refrain, are absent from the earliest witnesses and are widely regarded as harmonizations (scribal additions matching parallel passages) from verse 48. Their omission does not change the verdict because verse 48 retains the refrain in all major texts.

variants.note: No variant units supplied in the bundle for the anchor verses. Revelation 20:10, Revelation 14:11, Matthew 25:46, Daniel 12:2, and Mark 9:48 are outside the open-cbgm 3 John sample (the manuscript-comparison method's available reference corpus), so CBGM (Coherence-Based Genealogical Method, a statistical text-criticism tool) was not consulted. The verdict-relevant clauses in all anchors are textually stable in the principal critical editions.

competing_lens_verdicts.rationale: Reads 'they will be tormented unto the ages of the ages' (basanisthesontai eis tous aionas ton aionon) in Revelation 20:10, 'they have no rest day and night' (ouk echousin anapausin hemeras kai nyktos) in Revelation 14:11, 'does not die' (ou teleuta) and 'is not quenched' (ou sbennytai) in Mark 9:48, the 'eternal' (aionios) parallel in Matthew 25:46, and the post-resurrection 'everlasting abhorrence' (deraon olam) of Daniel 12:2 as predicating unending conscious experience of the punished. Treats 'destroy' (apollymi) in Matthew 10:28 in the metaphorical sense of ruining a person's flourishing, 'destruction' (olethros) in 2 Thessalonians 1:9 as ruinous separation rather than extinction, and 'the second death' of Revelation 20:14 as the apostolic metaphor for the alienated state of those already named as tormented in Revelation 20:10.

Reads the canon's reservation of 'immortality' (athanasia, 1 Corinthians 15:53 to 54, 1 Timothy 6:16) and 'incorruption' (aphtharsia) for the redeemed as structural: immortality is a gift to believers, not a natural endowment of every human soul. The wages of sin in Romans 6:23 is 'death' (thanatos), set in contrast to 'eternal life' (zoe aionios), with 'death' (thanatos) as the canon's primary cessation-of-life word. The lost therefore cease, not because the destruction language is metaphorical but because they were never made unending.

Reads 'destroy' (apollymi) active in Matthew 10:28 at its strong sense of putting out of existence, 'destruction' (olethros) in 2 Thessalonians 1:9 and 'destruction' (apoleia) in Philippians 3:19 and 2 Peter 3:7 as terminal destruction, the Isaiah 66:24 worm-and-fire as acting on 'corpses' (pegarim), the Sodom and Edom smoke-imagery as memorial of completed ruin rather than ongoing burning, and the explicit second death gloss (plain-English equation) of Revelation 20:14 as the apostle's own identification of the lake of fire. Construes 'eternal' (aionios) as qualifying permanence of result (eternal in effect, as the Sodom fire in Jude 7 is now extinct yet 'eternal' (aionios)), so the wicked are destroyed rather than kept conscious.

hermeneutics.notes: All three frameworks read the same lexemes ('eternal' (aionios), 'torment' (basanismos), 'destroy' (apollymi), 'destruction' (olethros), 'death' (thanatos), 'immortality' (athanasia), 'worm' (skolex)) in opposite directions. The decision turns on the sense selected for 'eternal' (aionios), whether durative (ongoing in time) or qualitative (belonging to the coming age), on whether torment-verbs and destruction-verbs describe one process or two phases, and on whether the canon's restriction of 'immortality' (athanasia) to the redeemed is structural or merely a positive-quality term. The lexical data underdetermines (does not by itself settle) the choice, hence the disputed verdict.

stem_audit.neutralized_form: Describe the lexical force of the final-state passages for the unjust (Matthew 25:46 'eternal punishment' (kolasin aionion), Revelation 14:11 and 20:10 'torment' (basanismos) and 'to torment' (basanizo), Mark 9:48 undying worm, Daniel 12:2 'everlasting abhorrence' (deraon olam)) alongside the destruction word-family ('destroy' (apollymi) in Matthew 10:28, 'destruction' (olethros) in 2 Thessalonians 1:9, 'destruction' (apoleia), the second death gloss (plain-English equation) of Revelation 20:14, and the canon's reservation of 'immortality' (athanasia) to the redeemed) and report whether Scripture's language indicates ongoing conscious punishment, terminal destruction of the person, or is materially contested between the two.
stem_audit.notes: The stem 'the wicked are not ultimately destroyed and reduced to non-existence; the punishment of the unjust in the final state is conscious and ongoing' is a denial-stem that builds in the eternal-conscious conclusion and prejudges the destruction word-family as non-literal. It also selects a contested sense of 'eternal' (aionios), the durative (ongoing-in-time) sense, without arguing for it. The neutralized form names the texts on both sides without presupposing which reading wins. The verdict is derived on the original stem and returned disputed precisely because the neutral framing exposes a live lexical contest in which the destruction terminology, expanded in this pass to include 'destroy' (apollymi, 93 New Testament), 'destruction' (apoleia, 19), 'death' (thanatos, 120, with the Revelation 20:14 gloss), and 'immortality' (athanasia, 3, restricted to God and the redeemed), is genuinely defensible from the words on the page. Verdict held consistent with the sibling doc-eternal-conscious-torment evidence, which records the same lexical contest from the opposite stem direction.

lay_summary: This question asks whether the Bible's words about the final fate of the wicked describe punishment that is conscious and unending, or whether the wicked are finally destroyed and cease to exist. The strongest torment words point toward ongoing conscious punishment. Revelation 20:10 says they will be tormented (basanisthesontai) to the ages of the ages. Revelation 14:11 says the smoke of their torment (basanismos) rises and they have no rest (anapausis) day or night. Mark 9:48 says the worm does not die and the fire is not quenched, using two ongoing present-tense verbs (ou teleuta and ou sbennytai). Matthew 25:46 sets eternal punishment (kolasin aionion) in the same grammar as eternal life (zoen aionion), so one word for duration, the adjective 'eternal' (aionios), covers both. Daniel 12:2 sets everlasting life beside everlasting abhorrence (deraon olam) for the raised dead. Read together these favor punishment that continues. But the picture is contested by another set of words. The verb in Matthew 10:28 says God can destroy (apolesai, from apollymi) both soul and body in hell (gehenna), and across the New Testament this verb spans senses from render-lost to put-to-death. Second Thessalonians 1:9 calls the end eternal destruction (olethron aionion), using a ruin word rather than a torment word. Revelation 20:14 gives its own plain-English equation of the lake of fire, calling it the second death (ho thanatos ho deuteros), using the canon's primary word for the end of life. Romans 6:23 names the wage of sin as death (thanatos), set against eternal life (zoe aionios), not as eternal torment. The word for immortality (athanasia) appears only three times in the New Testament and is granted only to God and to the redeemed at resurrection, suggesting that unending existence is a gift, not a default. The worm-and-fire image in Mark comes from Isaiah 66:24 where the worm and fire act on corpses (pegarim), not living sufferers. The adjective translated eternal (aionios) can mean either lasting forever or belonging to the age to come, and Sodom is called an example of eternal fire in Jude 7 even though it is no longer burning. The same vocabulary is honestly pulled in two directions. Both readings can be built from the words on the page, so the lexical evidence is best recorded as disputed, with the torment passages reading naturally as ongoing experience and the destruction vocabulary reading naturally as terminal end.
